prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the identification of its active form, which opened the way to incretin-based therapies for diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-achievement prize for B031 to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. Round 1 did not alter the scientific case, which rests on an unbroken chain from proglucagon processing and the incretin effect, through the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide and its human physiology, to receptor agonists with independently confirmed benefit on glycaemia, weight and cardiovascular and renal outcomes. It is mature enough that recognition is not premature, and the gut-to-brain appetite axis keeps it a physiological discovery and not only a drug story. I weigh it on originality, maturity and breadth, and I do not count the six-member convergence as evidence. The round-1 exchange tested the attribution more than the merit, and I find the discovery-level trio the most defensible reading of the supplied credit. The citation names the therapies that followed, so the omission of Knudsen is not read as a verdict on the drugs.
statement.case_against: Credit remains the weak point, and I cannot dissolve it from the supplied evidence. Mojsov's priority on the active peptide relative to the Habener group, who are not among the credited names, is contested, and I have only recollection of that record, as does every other member. The chair's first question asks whether the committee can settle it without recollection, and I do not think it can. A prize that omits Knudsen can look like physiology without the pharmacology that reached patients, and a prize that includes her displaces one of the discoverers. Long-term safety, durability of weight loss and newer indications are still being characterised, which affects the wording of the citation but not the discovery.

responses.point: You moved from B046 to the GLP-1 trio but asked that the citation name the therapies that followed, and that Mojsov's priority not be called settled because we all rely on recollection. You also said you weight demonstrated effect on human disease more heavily than I appeared to for optogenetics.
responses.response: I accept both points. I have reworded my citation to say that the identification of the active form opened the way to incretin-based therapies, so the clinical consequence is in the text without crediting the industrial step. I agree that Mojsov's priority is unverified in our supplied material, and I will not call it settled. My position is conditional: I credit Mojsov because the supplied credit lists her identification of the active peptide, and if that were shown to fail I would move to Knudsen as the third name, not to a different prize. On human disease effect I concede your point, which is why I keep optogenetics only as an alternative. A tool whose clinical use is just beginning should not be placed ahead of a discovery with demonstrated effect in millions of patients.

responses.point: As chair you asked whether the committee can settle Mojsov versus Habener without relying on recollection, and whether a two-part prize is preferable, given that a second part would force a cut inside the three-person cap.
responses.response: I do not think we can settle the priority question from the supplied evidence, and I would not pretend otherwise at the final ballot. What we can do is state the rule we apply, which is to credit the discovery-level contribution among the supplied names, and to say that this is a judgment about the supplied credit and not a ruling on Habener. On the second part, the cap decides it. Adding B016 or B042 would cut Drucker, Holst or Mojsov, and I would not weaken the strongest discovery chain on the list to assemble a broader headline. A single-achievement prize is my preferred configuration.

responses.point: You argued that the third slot should be decided as an explicit choice between discovery of the active peptide and development of long-acting analogues, because the two give different citations, and that channelrhodopsin work is a true discovery about a light-gated channel.
responses.response: I agree that the choice is between discovery and development, and that it should be recorded as a choice. I choose discovery because the identification of the active peptide is what made the later pharmacology rational, and the three-name cap forces a decision. On optogenetics I accept your correction that channelrhodopsin characterisation is a discovery about a light-gated channel and not only a tool, and I have kept my earlier wording to that effect. It does not change my ranking. The six-name credit leaves at least three credible people out of any trio, and I see no principled way to choose among Bamberg, Boyden, Miesenböck and Nagel, so it stays an alternative.

responses.point: You keep the unfolded protein response (B042) as a conceptually original, compactly credited fall-back if the GLP-1 credit cannot be defended, and you ask whether a two-part prize might serve better.
responses.response: The UPR is the cleanest basic-science case on the shortlist and I ranked it fourth for that reason. But the fall-back logic does not persuade me, because the GLP-1 attribution problem is a question about one name, and a defensible trio with a stated rule exists. The reason to prefer GLP-1 is that its human consequence is demonstrated, whereas the UPR's therapeutic payoff is still indirect and the mammalian PERK and ATF6 arms (Ron, Kaufman and others) are outside the credit. If the committee wanted a basic-science prize this year I would support Walter and Mori, but I would put that to a later year and not use it to hedge the GLP-1 decision.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, relative to the Habener group, holds up. I cannot verify it from the supplied evidence, and if it fails I would move to Knudsen as the third name.
Whether the prize should recognise drug development as well as physiology, and if so whether that belongs in the third slot or is left outside the cap.
How the citation should describe long-term safety, durability of weight loss and newer indications without overstating them.
Whether the six-name optogenetics credit makes it unsuitable regardless of merit, or whether some principle could choose three names fairly.
statement.conflict_note: No recusal issue is apparent for any shortlisted ballot. I co-authored a 2009 paper with Thomas Perlmann on stem-cell-derived dopamine neurons, and papers with Sten Grillner and Patrik Ernfors on other topics, none of which concerns a shortlisted discovery. My motor-circuit field uses optogenetics as a tool, and I have no documented involvement with any of the six credited optogenetics names, so I note it only as familiarity and I rank B019 as an alternative. Nothing in round 1 changes this disclosure.
